Problems & solutions

How do I start exercising when I’m very unfit?

Explore manageable starting points, pacing and ways to build confidence.

By Nutrition.Fitness · 15 September 2026 · 4 min read

The short answer

Begin with activity you can manage safely and repeat, even if that is a short walk or gentle seated movement. Choose a pace and starting point suited to your current ability. Build gradually rather than testing your limits. If you have been inactive for a long time or have medical concerns, ask your GP about an appropriate start.

You start by choosing something manageable for the body you have today. Being able to do a difficult workout is not an entry requirement. Neither is owning matching trainers, liking gyms or knowing what a burpee is.

If you have not exercised for some time, or you have medical conditions or concerns, the NHS recommends speaking to your GP first. An appropriate starting point depends on your circumstances. General beginner advice should not override rehabilitation guidance or an existing care plan.

Choose the easiest place to begin

“Easy” here means accessible and repeatable. You might prefer privacy at home, company in a beginner class or a familiar route near your house. There is no award for choosing the setting that makes you most uncomfortable.

Think about the practical details: safe flooring, a suitable chair, comfortable clothing, accessible toilets and whether you need someone with you. If the thought of entering a gym is the biggest hurdle, ask for a quiet-time visit before committing to membership. You can use that visit simply to see the space and ask questions.

Pick a starting activity you understand

If walking is accessible to you, choose a short familiar route with an easy way to turn back. The NHS walking guide advises inactive walkers to increase distance gradually. A route that ends near home is often a more practical experiment than setting off towards a distant landmark and hoping for the best.

If standing movement is difficult, look for an appropriate seated option and individual advice where needed. The NHS strength-exercise guide demonstrates gentle movements such as sit-to-stand and wall press-ups, with instructions on a stable chair and gradual progression. Use the actual demonstration and choose movements suitable for you; a list of exercise names alone is not enough instruction.

What a first week might involve

This is an example of organising a start, not a prescribed workout:

  • Choose one source of clear instructions so you are not comparing ten contradictory videos.
  • Pick a short, suitable activity and an achievable time to try it.
  • Notice whether the surroundings, instructions and pace work for you.
  • Repeat a manageable version before deciding it needs to be harder.
  • Write one sentence about what would make the next attempt easier.

Your sentence might be “I need a quieter room”, “I could not see the demonstration on my phone” or “The route had no place to rest”. Those are useful discoveries. A beginner programme should help you solve them, rather than interpret them as excuses.

Progress does not have to mean pushing harder immediately

At first, progress might mean knowing where to start, needing less setup or feeling comfortable repeating a movement. Once an activity feels manageable, a small change may be appropriate. That could involve duration, repetitions or resistance, depending on the activity and any professional guidance you have.

Do not change everything at once because the first session went well. Leave room to see how you feel later and the following day. Nor do you need to compare your starting point with somebody whose training history you do not know.

Distinguish a training question from a health question

“Where should I put my feet?” may be a question for an appropriately qualified instructor. New pain, faintness or unusual breathlessness is a reason to stop and seek suitable medical advice, rather than ask an app to push you through. If activity repeatedly causes a delayed, disproportionate worsening of symptoms, get individual advice instead of following a generic progression schedule.

A responsible provider should be comfortable saying that their general programme is not suitable for a particular need. Ask how they decide suitability and what they do if you struggle.

What you need to buy today

Possibly nothing. Comfortable clothes, a safe space and free instructions may be enough to test a starting routine. You do not need supplements or specialist equipment to earn the right to begin.

If you would value an organised programme, review the programme information and check the actual beginner options. If you need supervision or medical adaptation, consider the corresponding professional service. Choose one manageable next step, not a complete reinvention of your life by Monday.
